correctness.rationale: All N=2^d, d>=3, 4<=m<=N, distinct four-column supports are exhausted by two affine orbits. The plane orbit reduces to occupancy of four equally sized Walsh types; the independent orbit reduces to affine rank of eight cube vertices, with exactly 12 coplanar quadruples. Inclusion-exclusion gives both closed binomial formulas. For m^2/N->0, product asymptotics give the exponential ratio. Direct exact verifier reproduces all 70 supports and sampling sizes on N=8, two canonical supports and all sampling sizes on N=16, and all 12 cube planes; 450 assertions. Modular rank equals rational rank since 4x4 integer sign determinants have magnitude <=16, smaller than the modulus 101. Analytic proof, not finite enumeration, supports all dimensions.

originality.rationale: Claim-specific searches and material comparisons found no implication of the exact two-orbit rank-failure laws. Classic SRHT and block-SRHT primary sources establish general embedding bounds; Ipsen–Wentworth state generic coherence-dependent rank/conditioning estimates, not the class-specific binomial counts in the accessible material; older Sylvester leading-principal-submatrix spectral analysis has a different object. A four-sparse Walsh exact Fourier support classification excludes the null coefficient patterns responsible for the four-corner dependencies, and an eight-point orthogonal Walsh spectrum census is not an exact arbitrary-row four-column singularity probability. No claim of categorical publication novelty or independent audit is made; specialist minor-counting and inaccessible sources remain residual risk.

value.rationale: Rank loss is the sharp failure event for embedding a fixed coordinate subspace and a fundamental property of randomized numerical linear-algebra sketches. Four-coordinate supports are the first size exhibiting distinct affine types. The exact finite-N full-parameter laws reveal a substantial 9/2 failure-ratio already in dimension 8 and an exponential asymptotic separation even with identical leverage/coherence, a motivated benchmark that general bounds cannot resolve. This classification is nontrivial beyond a one-off finite census; it applies to all Walsh orders and admissible sample sizes. Not a claim about general condition numbers or runtime.
